item.title: Ukraine War Enters Its Fifth Winter
item.description: False narratives, low inventories and weak diplomacy are hurting Zelenskyy’s efforts and fueling Putin’s pursuit.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: Japan Raises the Bar on Residency. Cue the Outrage
item.description: From the US green card to the UK’s “indefinite leave to remain,” permanent residency in a country that’s not your own can be a prickly issue. Japan is now getting choosier about who gets to stay for good.
item.dc:creator: Gearoid Reidy

item.title: The Whole Indian Options Trade Was Too Good
item.description: Also compute futures manipulation, AI Ebitda add-backs and AI safety stereotypes.
item.dc:creator: Matt Levine

item.title: Hyrox Needs to Remember Who Its Customers Are
item.description: Hyrox takes its sporting credentials seriously — it was, after all, co-founded by an Olympian. But the commercial success of the high-endurance fitness race isn’t built on the backs of elite athletes. It comes from attracting overachieving gym junkies.
item.dc:creator: Juliana Liu

item.title: US Bonds and Tina Turner: What Is the True Price of Safety?
item.description: This article is adapted from Worth the Risk: The Seven Myths That Keep Us From Taking the Chances We Need to Take by Allison Schrager, to be published by Yale University Press. Copyright © 2026 by Allison Schrager. Excerpted by permission. All rights reserved.
item.dc:creator: Allison Schrager

item.title: Mexico's Superpeso Requires Careful Handling
item.description: A Big Mac in Mexico already costs almost $6.50. So does a gallon of premium gasoline. The shiny new iPhone 18 Pro? That will set you back 29,999 pesos, or about $1,765 at 17 to the dollar, nearly 50% more than the US pre-tax list price. And I won’t get into what private-school tuition costs in Mexico City even before converting it into dollars.
item.dc:creator: Juan Pablo Spinetto

item.title: Ossoff's Viral Clips Are Only Half the Story
item.description: Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff’s viral videos have so mastered the attention economy that the East Coast media is swooning with speculation that he could be a presidential contender in 2028. He has vigorously probed Trump administration officials during committee hearings. He coined the term “the Epstein class.” And he drew weeks of scrutiny to President Donald Trump’s close associate Natalie Harp with his derogatory quip about the president’s “travel with Natalie.”
item.dc:creator: Mary Ellen Klas

item.title: US Is Squandering its Global Leverage With Ukraine and Iran
item.description: President Donald Trump sees the art of geopolitics as a matter of money and leverage. As a result, he’s relied on fellow businesspeople to do the work of diplomats in Gaza, Ukraine and the Persian Gulf — and they have failed. As Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once put it, the revolution that founded the Islamic Republic of Iran “was not about the price of watermelons.”
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: AI Is Already Damaging Human Life. We Gave It a Head Start
item.description: The AI-industrial complex is in turmoil after several of its executives and engineers warned the technology could kill some or all humans, possibly before the 2036 election. This could be real cause for alarm or just brilliant marketing. Whatever the case, artificial intelligence is already harming humans through environmental devastation encouraged by the US government. We won’t need a decade to see the impact.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gongloff

item.title: Ukraine War: Putin Must Be Convinced Ending Conflict Is His Best Bet
item.description: Last week’s visit to Ukraine by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner appeared to achieve little: After they left Kyiv, Russian missiles again struck the Ukrainian capital, killing civilians and damaging homes, a school and a clinic. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s blunt forecast that the war looks set to continue into the winter was less a rejection of diplomacy than frank acknowledgement of its limits.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Democrats’ Chance to Flip the Senate Is Growing — But Not Certain
item.description: Figuring out why Democrats are poised to score a massive upset in the battle for control of the US Senate doesn’t require the computational power of AI: Gas costs more than $4 per gallon on average; diesel is running $6-plus; ground chuck is roughly $7 a pound — and a Republican occupies the White House.
item.dc:creator: David M. Drucker

item.title: AI Raises Biological Threats Faster Than Governments Can Respond
item.description: Anthropic PBC researcher Jacob Coxon quit last week and posted on social media that it was because “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Evan Hubinger, who leads the artificial intelligence company’s alignment science team, put the odds above 10% in the next 10 years. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the AI frontier to help mitigate the risks, an idea echoed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon M
item.dc:creator: Gautam Mukunda

item.title: Clearlake Todd Boehly: Are Chelsea Also-Rans Really Worth £5 Billion?
item.description: There are far less stressful ways to make a modest profit than dabbling in an English Premier League football club. So financier Todd Boehly must feel some relief to be leaving Chelsea FC without financial injury four years into a tough turnaround. He has handed US buyout firm Clearlake Capital full control — but control only counts for so much when you have limited freedom of movement.
item.dc:creator: Chris Hughes

item.title: The Fed Never Hikes Just Once? Alan Greenspan Disagreed
item.description: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Wednesday presided over the first US interest rate increase since 2023, and rate hikes are generally a package deal, as the aphorism goes. Versions of that folk wisdom circulated ahead of the decision, delivered by the likes of former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Jim Bullard and one-time Fed Vice Chair Richard Clarida. Their conviction is reflected in market pricing, with swaps traders anticipating around three more increases by late 202
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Levin

item.title: Warsh’s Fed Soars Like a Hawk Into a Hiking Cycle
item.description: Unanimity reveals a resolve that wasn’t there before.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: The French Election Is Ignoring the Bond Market
item.description: The chief executive officer of insurance company AXA SA, Thomas Buberl, didn’t mince words Tuesday about the severity of France’s debt problem as global bond yields rise and the country’s risk premium over Germany hits its highest level in more than a decade. He called for reforms to get public finances under control and said a proposal by the far left to cancel debt held at the central bank was “dangerous” and “play(ing) with fire.”
item.dc:creator: Lionel Laurent

item.title: AI Boom: How to Stop Data Centers From Taking Too Much Electricity
item.description: The rapid expansion of data centers has become one of the most tangible expressions of the artificial intelligence revolution. But debate about their environmental, economic and social impact threatens their future development. And rightly so. Although the digital economy is often seen as weightless, every cloud service and AI application depends on massive physical infrastructure that takes up land, consumes energy, uses water and requires ever-increasing investment.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Sanchez
